title: Egypt: End judicial harassment of Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Atallah
content:
Responding to the news that Lina Atallah, editor-in-chief of independent outlet Mada Masr, has been summoned to appear before Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution (SSSP) today for investigation in a new criminal case against her, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Regional Impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said:

“It is utterly disgraceful that the Egyptian authorities are once again targeting Lina Atallah for the brave and professional reporting by her team at Mada Masr. This is the sixth case against Mada Masr and its journalists in six years, illustrating the Egyptian authorities’ relentless harassment of independent journalists who challenge the state-controlled narrative.

“Lina Atallah has been bravely leading one of the few remaining independent media outlets in Egypt and should never have been targeted with these successive investigations. Egyptian authorities must immediately end all judicial harassment against her and Mada Masr staff.

title: States must act as Israeli state-driven settler violence escalates at the start of Palestinian olive harvest
content:
Responding to the latest acts of state-driven Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank over the weekend, which also targeted a delegation of European diplomats and a Washington Post photojournalist, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Heba Morayef, said:

“Once again, Israel’s apartheid system is turning the olive harvest into a season of horror for Palestinian families across the occupied West Bank. State-driven attacks by settlers on farmers that damage, destroy and steal crops, combined with Israeli military restrictions on access to groves, are causing immense suffering and economic loss for Palestinians.

“The series of attacks by settlers over the weekend against Palestinian residents of Khirbet Abu Falah and Taybeh in the Ramallah area, which also targeted a Washington Post photojournalist and a delegation of European diplomats, offer a glimpse into a reality of relentless aggression against Palestinians. Attempts by senior Israeli officials and electoral candidates across the political spectrum to portray this state-sponsored brutality as the work of a few individuals are a blatant distortion of reality.

title: Human Rights Education Resources for Write for Rights 2026
content:
Every year around 10 December – Human Rights Day – Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign brings millions of people together to stand in solidarity with individuals and communities facing human rights violations.

Around the world, people write letters, sign petitions, create artwork, learn together, and take action to demand justice. Year after year, these collective actions have helped change lives, showing that borders are no barrier to solidarity and that words have the power to inspire hope and drive change.

Human rights education is a central part of that movement. Alongside taking action, people come together to understand the issues behind each Individual at Risk case, reflect on why human rights matter and explore how solidarity can help protect them.

The Write for Rights 2026 Human Rights Education resources help teachers, educators and facilitators engage learners in meaningful learning about human rights and support them to take informed action.

title: India: End the crackdown on peaceful protests and release arbitrarily detained protesters
content:
The brutal crackdown on peaceful protesters in New Delhi over the last weekend is alarming with mass detention, unlawful use of force, the targeting of journalists, human rights defenders including lawyers, and internet shutdowns, said rights groups in a statement.

Amnesty International, CIVICUS, Front Line Defenders and South Asians for Human Rights call on the Indian authorities to release everyone arbitrarily detained for the exercise of their right to freedom of peaceful assembly and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces. 

On 10 October 2026, protests were called by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and backed by student groups calling for the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India, following reports that the nationwide Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls by the election commission removed around 130 million names from voter lists.

title: Kenya: Authorities must address economic grievances driving protests, end repressive tactics
content:
Kenyan authorities have increasingly used authoritarian tactics, including arbitrary arrests and detention, abductions, malicious prosecution of protesters, surveillance, and media repression, to crack down on protests against deepening economic hardship and the government’s aggressive fiscal policies, Amnesty International said in a new report today. 

The report, “Human Rights Under Siege: Unpacking Authoritarian Practices in an Era of Economic Pressure amid Youth-Led Protests in Kenya”, documents how between 2023 and 2025, increased food and transport costs, levies and tax hikes, high public debt, corruption, rising poverty and inequality, as well as broken electoral promises led to public anger and protests.

“The findings of this report are troubling and paint a stark picture of the Kenyan government’s repressive response to real grievances affecting the day-to-day lives of ordinary people,” said George Morara, Amnesty International Kenya’s Executive Director.

title: Azerbaijan: Stop denying access to education through discriminatory hijab restrictions and release peaceful protesters
content:
Reacting to the growing number of reports that peaceful activists protesting the school hijab ban have been detained and that an activist who attempted to organize free online lessons for girls affected by the uniform regulations has gone missing, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:

“Mass arrests of peaceful protesters alongside participants in violent riots, including the reported detention of a mother protesting against her daughter’s exclusion from school, and the disappearance of an activist who aimed to help affected girls, are typical of the state’s violent suppression of the lawful exercise of the right to protest peacefully, and the crackdown on freedom of expression and all dissent in Azerbaijan.

“Denying girls access to classrooms because they wear a hijab is discriminatory and violates their rights to education, and the freedoms of religion and expression. The secular character of public education doesn’t justify a blanket restriction on religious dress.

title: Portugal: Police violence against peaceful housing protesters must be investigated
content:
Initial reports suggest that the police deployed excessive force to disperse a peaceful protest camp in Porto, Portugal, in the early hours of 15 October that injured 37 people, said Amnesty International in a statement today.

“Reports of police violence against people peacefully protesting Portugal’s housing crisis are deeply troubling. People have the right to protest peacefully, including the right to occupy public space and including at night-time. The Portuguese authorities must respect and protect that right.

“Dispersal of peaceful protests must be a last resort. Reports that police beat protesters with batons resulting in dozens of people being injured, including a person with a disability, raise serious concerns that the use of force was disproportionate,” said João Godinho Martins, Executive Director of Amnesty International Portugal.

title: Norway: Proposed sovereign wealth fund reforms would mark biggest setback for its human rights safeguards in 20 years
content:
The new proposals to change the ethical framework governing Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global could significantly weaken independent human rights oversight, reduce transparency and make it harder to exclude companies linked to serious abuses, Amnesty International said today.

Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, is reviewing its ethical governance framework. The Gjedrem Committee, set up for this purpose, has proposed weakening the independent Council on Ethics, allowing some of its assessments to remain confidential, and making it harder to exclude companies linked to serious human rights risks.

“The proposed ethical governance changes in the Norwegian fund risk weakening accountability and integrity and dismantling key human rights protections and amount to the most significant weakening of its human rights safeguards in two decades. When the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund changes its standards, the consequences do not stop at Norway’s borders. Other investors pay attention, and companies do too,” said John Peder Egenæs, Secretary General of Amnesty International Norway.

title: “Every little boat here, every fisherman… is an act of resistance”
content:
For Alexandre Anderson de Souza and other artisanal fishers, Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, is a source of livelihood, identity and culture.

But pollution from multiple sources, including the oil and gas industry, industrial waste and untreated sewage has turned the bay into a sacrifice zone. Artisanal fishers face contaminated water, declining fish stocks, eroded mangrove, shrinking fishing areas and increasingly dangerous routes, while polluters profit without paying for the environmental degradation they cause.

Alexandre co-founded Associação Homens e Mulheres do Mar (Association of Men and Women of the Sea – AHOMAR), a network of artisanal fishers that has spent nearly two decades defending the bay and their traditional way of life from the impacts of oil and gas infrastructure. Several environmental human rights defenders (EHRDs) told Amnesty International that they feared for their safety, some facing intimidation and harassment.

title: India: Release CJP leaders arrested after attempting peaceful protests at Jantar Mantar
content:
The Delhi authorities must immediately release Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who have been remanded to five days of judicial custody after trying to protest at Jantar Mantar on Tuesday. Their arrests, following the removal of the site’s designation as an authorized protest venue, raise serious concerns about shrinking space for peaceful protest and dissent in India. 

According to a post on X by CJP’s legal head, Ratna Singh, Das and Ranka were remanded to judicial custody on Wednesday. Party member Ajinkya Shinde, who was also detained, was released on a personal bond of INR 5,000 (USD 55). A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against Das and Ranka under provisions relating to breach of bond, criminal trespass and disobedience of orders, among other charges. Shinde was also placed under preventive arrest before being released.
